extracted.intended_audience: students learning news writing / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and examples for teaching news-writing skills (clarity, tone, paragraphing, libel avoidance, factual precision) using sample stories to be corrected or analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the time relation entirely clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the following story for its excellence in keeping the time relation entirely clear. Show how the writer obtains this clearness ... (Paragraphs 124-131).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an unmistakable chronology in the narrative so readers can follow when events happened; use specific dates/times and sequence sentences so cause-effect and timing are unambiguous. The exercise asks students to show how the writer achieves clearness (example: Myrtle Reed story) and to point out structures that avoid temporal confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the possibility of libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Show how the writer avoids the possibility of libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish or rely on unverified accusatory statements or ambiguous evidence; identify and authenticate documents before using them (example: judge ruled the typewritten note 'was not sufficiently identified and rejected it as evidence'). Attribute claims to reliable sources and avoid presenting allegations as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct paragraphing (logical paragraph breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate the places at which paragraphs should be made in the following stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break text at logical shifts in topic, time, place, speaker, or action. Use paragraphing to improve readability and to signal changes in chronology or emphasis (Chapter XI exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate journalistic tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The following stories are lacking in tone. Correct them in any way necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an appropriate, professional news tone: avoid excessive flattery, mawkishness, mock-solemnity, archaisms, or sarcastic asides. Replace inflated, pompous, or melodramatic language with clear, restrained phrasing (many examples in section E illustrate florid or inappropriate tone to be corrected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and correct faults in stories (grammar, clarity, accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate and correct the faults in the following stories (paragraphs 131-134).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit for grammatical correctness, clarity, logical flow, factual accuracy, and readability. Exercises require pinpointing specific faults (awkward constructions, tense errors, wrong word choice) and providing corrected versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid redundancy and awkward repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticize passages that repeat information or use needless phrasing (example: 'An even one hundred reservations have been made ... and thirty have been made ... The management ... also says that patrons will be given the very best of service').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate repeated statements, tighten sentences, and avoid pleonasm. Combine or rephrase duplicated details so each sentence adds new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, concise, factual reporting; avoid melodrama and sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite stories that use hyperbolic, romantically florid, or sensational language (examples throughout 'lacking in tone' and F: 'death drew aside its mask of horror', 'moan and groan', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simple declarative sentences that state facts plainly. Remove rhetorical flourishes, overwrought metaphors, and needless dramatization so the news reads as reliable information rather than ornate prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose balanced, practical remedies when offering editorial comment
rubrics_metrics.description: In an editorial-like passage about a coasting fatality: 'The authorities should put a stop to it in Bowman, but at the same time the city should make safe provision for such sport by erecting toboggan slides ...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moving from reporting to editorial suggestion, present balanced, constructive recommendations: recognize the problem and propose feasible, measured solutions rather than only criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report official/legal actions and outcomes accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Report judicial orders, official findings, and procedural requirements precisely (example: Judge Windes refused to depose McCullough as administrator, ordered a definite report, and required a $50,000 bond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering courts or official actions, state exactly what was ordered, refused, or required, and avoid ambiguous or weasel wording. Attribute rulings to the proper official and include relevant specifics (amounts, duties, restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish unverified private correspondence or unidentified documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The typewritten note offered in evidence was rejected as not sufficiently identified; exercises emphasize caution about such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify provenance and authenticate private letters or notes before publishing; if evidence is disputed or not properly identified, do not present its contents as established fact. Attribute carefully and note disputes or court rulings when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be able to judge stories and explain reasons (critique and justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercises ask students to rewrite bad stories and to 'Show why the others are good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a story, identify the specific criteria (clarity, tone, accuracy, paragraphing, chronology, libel safety) that make it good or bad and justify edits with concrete examples from the text.
